units.translation: First, turning yourself toward the rising of the sun, walk over the unplowed fields.
with many eyes watching my tracks.
Alas, the bed and the tracks that love a man.
And indeed the tracks of feet are similar.
They come together into the same place as my tracks.
a spotted wing will again flutter around him.
providing a dense column of war.
There are no examples of the nominative singular στίξ [row], and oblique cases are rare: on this see Thes. vol. 7 p. 775.
how they two wrought many things upon the citizens and the ranks of all strangers.

where the scholiast says: ἐφεξῆς λέγοιμι, στοιχομυθοίην [I would speak in order, I would converse in sequence]. The verb is no more known from elsewhere than στοιχομυθεῖν [to converse in sequence], which Hesychius and Photius noted, interpreting it as τὸ ἑξῆς λέγειν [to speak in order].
if I should narrate in order for ten days (στιχηγοροροίην in several copies).
I would speak in order, I would converse in sequence
Schol. κατὰ στοῖχον ἔδειξα· πολλὰ γὰρ εἴδη μαντικῆς, εἰκαστικὸν, ἐπιπνευστικόν, ἀστρονομικόν [I showed in order; for there are many kinds of divination: by conjecture, by inspiration, by astronomy].
I arranged in order many modes of divination.
I showed in order; for there are many kinds of divination: by conjecture, by inspiration, by astronomy
to arrange the dense column of ships in three rows
garment, clothing. Hesychius explains it by ἔνδυμα [garment] and περιβόλαιον [wrap]. Often thus in Sophocles and Euripides, twice in Aeschylus.
Hesychius: στολή [garment]: πορεία, κίνησις [journey, movement]. Thus.
and she was arrayed in this garment.
do you see this remnant of my garment?
not swift is the equipment of a naval army.

Thus Heimsoethius for πρόστερνοι στολμοὶ πέπλων [breast-coverings of robes], deleting the gloss πέπλων [of robes] that had once been added to στολμῶν [of garments], which the scholiast had not noticed, who interpreted it as στολισμοὶ τῶν ὑφασμάτων [arrangements of the fabrics].
It is said of sails. Where the scholiast says: κατὰ περίφρασιν τὸ λαῖφος [by periphrasis, the sail].
and the coverings of the sail and the side-screens of the ship.
forces that are sent, i.e. army
a gathering of people who come together to lead a procession or to undertake a journey
Bothius rightly corrected to ἀνελληνόστολον [not Greek-equipped].

about which Pollux 1, 86 says: τὸ δὲ μεταξὺ τοῦ ἐμβόλου καὶ τῆς προεμβολίδος ὁ στόλος ἐστὶν ὑπὲρ τὴν στεῖραν, ὃς καὶ περικεφαλαία καλεῖται [the part between the ram and the fore-ram is the στόλος [beak], above the keel, which is also called περικεφαλαία [helmet]], and other grammarians indicated in Thes. vol. 7 p. 802.

where the scholiast says: τὸν ἔμβολον λέγει. στόλον δὲ λέγει παρ᾽ ὅσον εἰς ὀξὺ συνεσταλμέναι εἰσίν· οὕτως γὰρ ἔλεγον στόλον τὰ ἀπωξυμμένα [he means the ram. He calls it στόλον [beak] because they are drawn to a point; for thus they called pointed things στόλον].
